/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.headline: Aspiring Reform MP who said ‘you cannot be Muslim and British’ suspended
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.excerpt: An aspiring Reform UK MP who advocated the use of concentration camps and said “you cannot be Muslim and British” has been suspended from the party. The activist is one of a number featured in an ITV documentary, which will be broadcast in full on Sunday night and has already resulted in fresh questions about Reform’s vetting process. The year-long investigation included undercover filming at an event referred to as Farage Fest, which was thrown by the party to thank volunteers who helped Nigel Farage get re-elected as the MP for Clacton during the recent byelection. Those attending included Jason Powell, who said he had passed vetting checks to become a Reform parliamentary candidate, and who was recorded as saying: “Anyone who comes across on a boat, as an example, in the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you’re in there. “And that’s the first, the very first day … They just need to be rounded up, every single last one of them, and sent to those concentration camps, and then be given an ultimatum. Where are you from? Because you’re going back there. If you don’t tell us, you’re staying here for the rest of your life.” Powell was also recorded as saying that he was “pretty hardline about Islam as well”, adding: “I would have disagreements, especially with, um, I mean, as far as I understand, Zia Yusuf [Reform’s home affairs spokesperson] is a Muslim.
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.trail: Jason Powell also backed concentration camps as Reform councillors talk of executing grooming gang members

/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.headline: Jenrick claims Farage has done more to stand against racism than ‘almost anybody’
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.excerpt: Robert Jenrick has sought to defend Reform UK against fresh allegations that it hosts extremists by claiming that Nigel Farage has “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism and the far right”. The remarks came after Farage was berated by a Reform official for “protecting” a mayoral candidate who was accused of making racist remarks about the former Labour deputy prime minister David Lammy. The exchange emerged in an undercover investigation by ITV Exposure, which has also shown councillors and election candidates for Reform making threats of extreme violence and expressing racist, Islamophobic and misogynistic views. In the latest footage released by ITV, a senior Reform official is seen warning Farage that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about Lammy. Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, is also seen complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”. Jenrick, the party’s Treasury spokesperson and MP for Newark, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday: “[Farage] is the most heavily scrutinised figure in British politics, and he’s someone who’s probably done more than almost anybody else to stand against racism and the far right, and to protect our politics from that over the course of my lifetime.
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.trail: Reform MP defends leader after ITV footage shows official warning Farage he is ‘protecting’ candidate over racist David Lammy comments

/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.headline: UK ‘an outlier in Europe’ for letting Farage and other politicians present TV shows
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.excerpt: The UK has been confirmed as an outlier in Europe for allowing Nigel Farage and other serving politicians to present TV shows covering current affairs, according to an unprecedented analysis of broadcasting rules. Farage is one of a series of Reform UK figures who are permitted to present shows on the rightwing network GB News. The Reform MP Lee Anderson and former candidate Matt Goodwin also have regular slots on the channel. Their status as presenters has led to repeated concerns about the enforcement of Britain’s rules on impartial broadcasting. Last month, Farage used his first GB News show for six months to defend his party’s decision to accept two record £36m donations from the crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo. However, an international study has confirmed that the UK’s decision to allow politicians to present such shows is highly unusual across Europe. In 35 of the 37 European nations studied, regulators found no recent examples of serving politicians presenting news or current affairs programmes. Only Iceland, which has a population of about 400,000 people, and Malta bucked the trend. In Malta, political parties are even permitted to own television channels. There have been instances where MPs have presented interview programmes, although according to its regulator these are not the norm.
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.trail: Analysis of countries’ broadcasting rules confirms Ofcom code is highly unusual, amid concerns about impartiality

/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.headline: Farage accused of ‘protecting’ Reform candidate over racist slurs against David Lammy
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.excerpt: Nigel Farage was told by a senior Reform official that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about David Lammy, an undercover investigation has revealed. The latest footage from an undercover investigation by ITV also shows Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”. Other footage shows Farage himself discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party. The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged that he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds do not have a primary loyalty towards the UK. However, while Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, clips from an ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier disucussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”. “He needs to go, I’m getting rid of him,” Sumner was filmed saying when the controversy broke last December.
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.trail: Exclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’

/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.headline: Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and misogynist comments
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.excerpt: Reform UK has been rocked by a fresh crisis after councillors and election candidates for the party were caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views. Three councillors have already stood down from the party, which said it was conducting an investigation over the first revelations from an ITV undercover investigation that aired on Wednesday. Reform leader Nigel Farage has postponed a major announcement that was due to take place in Essex on Thursday morning as the party tries to contain the fallout expected to come from further revelations in the coming days. That will include revelations from undercover filming of senior Reform politicians and officials working at its UK headquarters. Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election. However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites,” and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. Feeney won seats on Birmingham city council and Solihull Metropolitan borough council and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. He has announced that he has left Reform “for personal reasons”.
/politics/2026/oct/19/farage-claim-that-.trail: Party faces fresh crisis as three councillors quit after ITV undercover filming exposed violence, misogyny and racist views

/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.headline: ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.excerpt: New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election. Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard (FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week. The announcement gained little attention compared to her inheritance tax bombshell, but it would have more far-reaching impacts on a greater number of people. The UK is in need of approximately 6m new homes and failing to equip them with efficient and low-carbon energy sources would doom households to higher bills for decades to come. The Tories quoted estimates of £30,000 for new-build houses, but the real cost is likely to be much less. Installing heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and insulation costs about £5,000 to £8,000 at the point of building – a figure estimated in 2024 when energy prices were much lower – to save more than £1,300 a year on bills, a saving likely to be substantially higher now. To retrofit homes after building would cost more than £20,000. Jan Rosenow, a professor of climate and energy policy at the University of Oxford, said: “Every home constructed today that runs on fossil fuels is a liability for the occupants. It also results in investor uncertainty and disrupts the supply chain that has been gearing up for this.
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.trail: Tories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on hold

/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.headline: Andy Burnham: UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.excerpt: The UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050, Andy Burnham has argued in his strongest comments yet on the issue, saying it is no longer possible for Britons to believe they are not already affected by a changing climate. Writing for the Guardian about new plans for a mass of community-led local green energy projects, the prime minister said the UK must “believe in itself”, and set out his determination to reach net zero targets, which have been rejected by the Conservatives and Reform UK. The tone marks a contrast to the summer, when Burnham faced criticism for a seemingly muted response to the heatwaves, droughts and wildfires that affected the UK, with his main initiative being a ban on portable barbecues. “I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050,” Burnham said. “I want Britain to believe in itself again.” Saying he wanted to connect local communities to green power projects – to reach net zero targets and make energy more affordable – Burnham said: “I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record.” He went on: “Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. “The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now.
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.trail: Exclusive: PM, who is facing pressure over whether to approve North Sea oil and gasfields, makes strongest comments yet on issue

/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.headline: Taxpayers to fund clear-up of illegal dumps in West Yorkshire, Surrey and Kent
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.excerpt: Illegal dumps in West Yorkshire, Surrey and Kent will be cleared up using taxpayer money, Andy Burnham has announced, as the prime minister promises a new drive to tackle toxic waste. Ministers have identified dumps in Bradford, Runnymede and the Isle of Sheppey, which collectively contain about 22,000 tonnes of illegal waste, to be cleared in the next phase of the government’s national clear-up effort. Meanwhile, fines will be raised for rogue dumpers, and AI-powered drones will be used to detect illegal activity while it happens, as the government looks to prioritise prevention alongside clean-up efforts. Burnham said in a statement: “These toxic dumps have blighted communities for too long. I said we would clean them up – and that’s exactly what we’re announcing today.” He added: “These mountains of rubbish have been a clear sign to communities that politics hasn’t been working for them or their area. This government is going to tackle the issues that have been ignored by Westminster for too long and bring back hope.” Hundreds of illegal waste sites have been reported across England, with a BBC investigation recently uncovering 11 “supersites” that contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish. One of the country’s most notorious sites is in Burnham’s own constituency of Makerfield, where a rotting, rat-infested mountain of waste has remained for more than 20 months.
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.trail: Andy Burnham promises drive to tackle toxic waste, raise fines and use AI-powered drones to detect illegal activity

/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.headline: Labour ‘could lose up to 50 seats’ to Greens if new drilling in North Sea approved
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.excerpt: Labour could lose dozens of seats to the Green party if the government allows new drilling in the North Sea, according to internal research shared with the Guardian. Green party analysis suggests up to 50 Labour MPs, including Andy Burnham’s key ally Louise Haigh, could lose their seats at the next election if the government fails to make urgent climate action a priority or allows new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea. The research found that voters in these key Labour v Green seats want bold action to tackle the climate crisis, which has contributed to record heatwaves, devastating wildfires and crippling droughts this summer in the UK – and say Labour MPs will pay the price if the demands are not met. Rachel Millward, a deputy leader of the Green party, said: “If Labour won’t be swayed by the science or the moral imperative to leave all fossil fuels in the ground, perhaps they will listen to the polling. “The data is clear: voters want more from our government on climate change, and they certainly don’t want our new prime minister to back away from his party’s bare minimum commitments.” Labour dismissed the claims, pointing out that since Burnham took office the number of seats the Green party is projected to win at the next election had fallen from 20 to seven.
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.trail: Greens say analysis shows government failure to take bold climate action could lead to big gains for party at election

/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.headline: Thom Yorke, Romy and Brian Eno among 200 musicians urging PM to reject new North Sea drilling
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.excerpt: More than 200 musicians including Massive Attack and Brian Eno have written to Andy Burnham urging him to reject plans for more oil and gas drilling in the North Sea. The letter, signed by 211 artists such as Bobby Gillespie, Olly Alexander and Paris Paloma, called on the prime minister to reject the Rosebank oilfield, warning that the project would fail to lower energy bills or provide energy security as most of the oil was likely to be exported. Other performers who put their name to the missive include Radiohead’s Thom Yorke, Ed O’Brien and Philip Selway; the Cure’s Robert Smith; Bobby Gillespie of Primal Scream; Alexis Taylor of Hot Chip; Anoushka Shankar, Kevin Rowland, Anna Calvi, Jacob Collier, David Gray, the electronic duo Bicep and the xx singer Romy. The government’s consultation on the project, which lies about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands, closed on Monday. Ministers will now decide on its future as well as that of the Jackdaw gasfield off Aberdeen, whose consultation concluded a week ago. Adura, the company behind both projects, has said the projects would result in £10.8bn in investment and support 3,500 jobs at the peak of construction, with 880 employees over its production lifetime. However, environmental activists argue that extracting fossil fuels from the UK’s largest remaining untapped oilfield will accelerate climate chaos.
/politics/2026/oct/19/burnham-urges-offi.trail: Robert Smith, Olly Alexander and Paris Paloma also among signatories to letter saying exploitation of Rosebank and Jackdaw fields defies climate reality

/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.headline: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.excerpt: As Republicans confront mounting political headwinds ahead of November’s midterm elections, Donald Trump is attempting to turn unrest in France into a cautionary tale for American voters, recasting the demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living as evidence of the dangers of immigration and the erosion of western civilization. At a rally in Kansas on Monday evening, Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”. “If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” he said. Nationwide protests in France on Saturday were called over rising fuel prices and falling purchasing power, and in several cities they erupted into looting and clashes with police that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests. On Monday, overnight curfews were issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris. “This is what’s happening to France – they want to happen to our country. It’s never happening here,” Trump declared, drawing loud cheers from the thousands-strong crowd in ruby-red Kansas where the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.trail: President at Kansas rally tries to turn protests into cautionary tale for US as Republicans face midterm losses

/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.headline: Why are people protesting across Europe?
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.excerpt: Young people have been taking to the streets across Europe, including in Spain, France and Portugal, to protest over their unhappiness at the state of schools and the wider cost of living crisis. In France, high school pupils have clashed with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, dilapidated classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. Pupils routinely miss months of teaching due to unfilled staff absences. Other demonstrators soon joined in, voicing their unhappiness about rising living costs, including over fuel prices after US bombing in effect caused the closure of the strait of Hormuz. The General Confederation of Labour, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the protests and called for lower prices, higher pensions and boosted wages. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, is nearing the end of his time in the Élysée Palace after serving two terms. Over the Pyrenees in Spain, activists took to the streets in September over housing prices. The protests were triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after an investment fund hiked her rent by 230%. Maricarmen Abascal died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital. Protesters have called for rent freezes, halting the evictions of vulnerable people and the regulation of short-term and room rentals. Similar pleas were made across the Iberian border in Portugal on Saturday, when hundreds gathered in central Lisbon.
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.trail: School conditions, unaffordable housing and the cost of living have brought demonstrators on to the streets in several countries

/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.headline: Ferocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolation
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.excerpt: The near-universal chorus of condemnation that greeted Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday, after one of the most violent days of rioting and looting in France’s recent history, was a stark reflection of just how weakened he now is. Speaking from his office at the Élysée Palace, the president delivered an eight-minute speech expressing “anger and shame” after a weekend in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured. A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement. Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille. Macron acknowledged the “deep anxiety” of young people but offered no concrete policy initiatives, no cabinet reshuffle and no new public spending, merely telling his prime minister to organise consultations and asking opposition politicians to take a stand. The response, across the political spectrum, was damning.
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.trail: French president has compounded impression of arrogance with strategic errors – and consequences could be profound

/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.headline: France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.excerpt: France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country. The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt. The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds rose by as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall, and the bond market sell-off pushed France’s borrowing costs close to a 24-year high. This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards its highest level in 14 years. Analysts at Goldman Sachs said European sovereign risk was back in focus, with fiscal concerns about France raising the question of whether there could be a repeat of the eurozone debt crisis of 15 years ago. “The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. But the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15,” the investment bank said. “The issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk remains unresolved in the euro area, requiring credible fiscal consolidation.” The two-year French bond yield rose by nine basis points to 3.64%.
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.trail: Difference between French and German borrowing costs widens after public buildings burned and shops looted

/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.headline: ‘It looks like a war zone’: France reels as looting continues for second night
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.excerpt: Just before 1am on Monday morning, two motorbikes carrying one passenger each stopped at a traffic light on a backstreet near rue de Rivoli, one of central Paris’s busiest shopping streets. “You’ve got to go where there are a lot of people, where they’ve done the shop windows,” said one motorbike rider to another. Minutes later 10 other men, their faces covered with ski balaclavas, came down the street on foot pursued by a police van. Soon after Emmanuel Macron’s televised speech on Sunday night telling the nation it was “unbearable to see our streets ransacked”, groups of men looted shops in central Paris for hours for a second night running. Dozens of people attempted to smash windows near Les Halles shopping centre and grab goods. Others broke into an electrical shop in Belleville in the north of the city. “Men were battering shop windows, trying to break in, then they were chased by police,” said a 73-year-old woman near Les Halles. “There were different groups running everywhere with police chasing on foot or by car, and at the same time, some people were setting bins and bikes alight. The groups breaking into shops aren’t hostile to passersby so you’d see local residents walking down the street on their way home late at night, and masked teenagers running past in the other direction carrying looted goods.
/world/2026/oct/19/french-police-lost-co.trail: Police appear to have been taken by surprise by scale of looting that began after protests turned violent in Paris and other cities

/money/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-new-rule.headline: UK petrol prices hit highest level in almost four years as bank holiday getaway looms
/money/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-new-rule.excerpt: UK petrol prices have hit their highest level since 2022, piling more financial pressure on motorists before the bank holiday weekend. The average cost of petrol has reached 161.6p a litre, while diesel costs an average of 183.4p a litre, according to the AA breakdown company. The last time the petrol price was so high was in November 2022, when it soared in the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. It comes as millions of people prepare to make car journeys over the bank holiday weekend, which will be marked in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. The RAC estimates that the UK’s motorways and major roads could have the most traffic since its records began in 2015. The services company has predicted Friday is likely to be the worst day for heavy traffic, with more than 4.1m cars expected on the roads. Luke Bosdet of the AA said the rise in petrol prices showed that “UK pump pricing is back to its worst”. It is “too often overpriced and uncompetitive, with too many communities denied road fuel at a reasonable price”, he said. The UK’s competition regulator told fuel retailers this year that it would step up its monitoring of pump prices amid concern over profiteering as the US war with Iran drives up wholesale costs. Before the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel. It hit a peak of $126 a barrel in April, before dipping to $71 at the start of July on hopes of a peace deal.
/money/2026/oct/19/andy-burnham-new-rule.trail: Average cost of petrol reaches 161.6p a litre, while diesel costs average of 183.4p, according to the AA

/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.headline: Unpolished, anti-Bibi, but evasive on peace: who is the Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot?
/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.excerpt: He has been called the man who is everything the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, is not. Gadi Eisenkot, a former general and the main opposition candidate in Israel’s elections this month, is unpolished where Netanyahu is slick. To Israelis he is both menschy (decent) and schlumpy (unkempt), his crumpled appearance contrasting with Netanyahu’s hair rinse, makeup and obsessive need to control his media depiction. In the Israeli commentator Anshel Pfeffer’s framing, he is the anti-Bibi among a roster of wanna-Bibis. And in an era of Israeli politics that has been defined by betrayals, dirty tricks and public and private smears, Eisenkot’s brand is rectitude. He only entered politics four years ago, and the name of his party – Yashar – means “straight” or “honest”. But on key issues, an Israel under Eisenkot may not look very different, as he has been non-committal on crucial issues – including the two-state solution and Israeli settlement of the occupied West Bank. “He’s not sleek. He’s not corrupt. I think he’s going to be looking more inwards than outwards. Because he’s a military guy, he’s interested in calming the waters,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst for the International Crisis Group. “[But] he’s hedging a lot.” For many voters, Eisenkot’s appeal is less about ideology than the vibe around him. Key to his appeal, said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political analyst, is his “very modest background”.
/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.trail: The ‘menschy’ former general contrasts with the current PM when it comes to style and character – yet on key policy points retains a studied ambiguity

/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.headline: New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements
/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.excerpt: The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners. The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person. Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation. The Israeli government closed the UK consulate last week in protest, forcing it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government. The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it. Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement. The proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications.
/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.trail: Global human rights commitments adopted by government extend reach to enablers of unlawful activity

/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.headline: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’
/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.excerpt: Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel. The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza. The Metropolitan police said 20 arrests had been made, including for criminal damage after demonstrators climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial, having Palestine Action placards, making a Nazi salute and assaulting police as officers made arrests. Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.
/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.trail: Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful

/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.headline: ‘Self-imposed irrelevance’: why the EU is failing to act on growing public criticism of Israel
/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.excerpt: When the British government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements and condemned “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank by state-backed “settler terrorists”, some EU diplomats hoped this dramatic shift in UK government policy towards Israel would have a galvanising effect on the rest of Europe. So far, it has not. Although France and Canada joined the UK in pledging to ban goods from illegal settlements and impose sanctions on “those who facilitate them or profit from them”, there has not yet been a wider ripple effect. A meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers on Monday is likely to showcase the bloc’s stasis in policy towards Israel – a stalemate that is at odds with rising public criticism in Europe of Israel’s government. A survey of 10 European countries, including Spain, France and Sweden, found large majorities of people had a negative opinion of Israel. Views had become more negative compared with the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center, mostly after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which unleashed a new crisis in the Middle East and a global economic shock. In Poland, negative views jumped eight points to 70% of respondents, in Italy they increased by nine points to 75% and in Germany they also rose by nine points to 73%. Israel is facing ever deeper isolation in the theatre of public opinion.

/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.headline: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
/world/2026/oct/19/israeli-police-detain.excerpt: Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving the region, with only seven to remain in the building. Among those leaving is the consul general, Helen Winterton. The change was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last month to ban trade with illegal settlements and introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those who aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two-state solution as the best means of ending the Israel-Palestine conflict. Miliband has also backed away from a threat to expel a parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign. There has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, before polls on 27 October if they appear to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics. Israel had ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed.

/technology/2026/oct/19/ai-tool-predict-.headline: As US medical debt grows, AI will be used more to collect it
/technology/2026/oct/19/ai-tool-predict-.excerpt: Medical debt is expected to grow in coming years as Republican-led health cuts come into force this winter. As it does, a changing world of medical billing and debt collection awaits patients: one where artificial intelligence increasingly listens, codes, bills and collects. Artificial intelligence takes notes in exam rooms, codes visits, sends out billing messages and powers AI agents who text patients in billing portals – all changing the debt-collection ecosystem. Medical debt will grow among “both the insured and uninsured, because of how we’re increasingly putting more costs onto individuals for those plans”, said April Kuehnhoff, a senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center. “It’s people who lose their coverage because they can’t afford it, or they can’t meet these new stringent requirements. It’s people who maybe they can afford it but the plan they get isn’t as good, and they are asked to have a higher deductible, higher co-pay, so they just have a higher out-of-pocket [cost],” she said. A report released last Tuesday found that more than one in four US adults reported they owed a medical debt in 2025. The proportion was the same – about one in four – for people with health insurance, according to an analysis by the Urban Institute and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. AI company leaders, such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, have promised to cure all diseases in a decade.

The company is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over the London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. Watson told the BBC podcast Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: “One of the things I’d say to my former colleagues is: do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?

/technology/2026/oct/19/ai-tool-predict-.headline: RFK Jr outlines expansive vision for collecting US health data at Maha event
/technology/2026/oct/19/ai-tool-predict-.excerpt: Robert F Kennedy Jr laid out an expansive vision for collecting, sharing and analyzing US health information at a Maha event hosted by a close ally and outspoken anti-vaccine activist. Medical and lifestyle data, from doctor’s visits to exercise, should be connected and shared with the government and independent researchers, where it can be searched by AI – including potential links between vaccines and health outcomes including autism and mortality, suggested Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine skeptic. “We need to use America’s health data to determine whether the food we eat, the chemicals we encounter, the vaccines that we’re administering, the other environmental and lifestyle exposures are contributing in one way or another to the chronic disease epidemic,” Kennedy said at an event with the Maha Institute on Monday, with about two dozen people tuning into the live stream. The Maha Institute is headed by Mark Gorton, who called himself “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference” two weeks ago. The institute was co-founded by Tony Lyons, whose publishing house gave $4m to Kennedy through various Maha foundations with funding from political contributions and health-related corporations, according to reporting by the New York Times.

/technology/2026/oct/19/ai-tool-predict-.headline: AI will help find cure for cancer ‘within our lifetimes’, says Arm Holdings chief
/technology/2026/oct/19/ai-tool-predict-.excerpt: The boss of one of the UK’s biggest chip companies has claimed AI will be able to find a cure for cancer “in our lifetime”. Rene Haas, chief executive of the chip designer Arm Holdings, said that, while modelling how a DNA marker is affected by cancer was currently “too complex” a problem for either humans or technology, computers were “going to solve it” in the future. Haas told the BBC: “AI is going to … find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer. “Modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer – it’s too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. “However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they’re going to solve it.” Scientists are already using AI-driven tools in cancer research and testing. Earlier this year, the NHS said more than 4 million patients received faster lung diagnosis thanks to funding in AI-powered X-ray tools. Haas added that AI would also pave the way for widespread humanoid robots within the next five years, but that chip shortages were stunting growth in the area. “With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks,” he said.
